name: Code of Hammurabi Stele
description: Basalt stele inscribed with 282 Babylonian laws beneath a relief of Hammurabi receiving authority from the sun-god Shamash. Looted to Susa in antiquity, excavated in 1901, now in the Louvre — the most complete early law code known.

name: Mask of Tutankhamun
description: Eleven-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis and glass, found on the pharaoh's mummy in his nearly intact tomb by Howard Carter in 1922 — the emblem of Egyptian archaeology.

name: Rosetta Stone
description: Granodiorite decree of Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek, found by French engineers in 1799. The parallel texts let Champollion crack hieroglyphs in 1822, unlocking three millennia of Egyptian records.

name: Terracotta Army
description: Some eight thousand life-size clay soldiers, horses, and chariots — each face individual — buried guarding Qin Shi Huang's tomb near Xi'an and rediscovered by well-diggers in 1974.

name: Antikythera Mechanism
description: Corroded bronze gearwork from a Greek shipwreck, revealed by X-ray tomography as an astronomical computer predicting eclipses and planetary positions — mechanical sophistication unmatched for a further millennium.

name: Book of Kells
description: Insular Gospel manuscript of virtuosic illumination — spiralling initials, interlace, and iconography — produced by Columban monks and displayed at Trinity College Dublin.

name: Bayeux Tapestry
description: Seventy-metre embroidered narrative of the Norman Conquest, from Harold's oath to his death at Hastings — part propaganda, part unique visual record of eleventh-century ships, arms, and dress.

name: Magna Carta (1215 exemplars)
description: Four surviving parchment engrossments of the charter King John sealed at Runnymede, held by the British Library and the cathedrals of Lincoln and Salisbury — physical anchors of constitutional tradition.

name: Gutenberg Bible
description: The first substantial book printed with movable metal type in Europe, in an edition of about 180; some 49 copies survive. Its typography set the standard the manuscript age could not match in speed or price.

name: Mona Lisa
description: Leonardo's portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, celebrated for its sfumato modelling and elusive expression; its 1911 theft from the Louvre made it the world's most famous painting.

name: Darwin's Beagle Specimens
description: The finches, mockingbirds, fossils, and notebooks Darwin collected on the Beagle voyage — the evidentiary seed of On the Origin of Species, dispersed today across the Natural History Museum, Cambridge, and Kew.

name: Wright Flyer
description: The Wrights' spruce-and-muslin biplane that made the first controlled, powered, heavier-than-air flights at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903 — twelve seconds and 36 metres on the first attempt. Displayed at the Smithsonian.

name: Enigma Machine
description: German rotor cipher machine whose military traffic Polish and then British cryptanalysts at Bletchley Park broke — an intelligence triumph credited with shortening the Second World War and seeding modern computing.

name: Apollo 11 Command Module Columbia
description: The only portion of the Apollo 11 stack to return to Earth, carrying Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins home from the first Moon landing; preserved at the Smithsonian.
